biomarker_rules.description: Leukopenia (normal or low WBC despite high fever)

overview: Enteric fever (commonly caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi) classically presents with a paradoxically low or normal white blood cell count (relative leukopenia) accompanied by persistent fever, mild liver enzyme irritation (elevated ALT/AST), and slight platelet reduction. It requires definitive microbiological confirmation.
suggested_follow_up_tests: Blood Culture for Salmonella enterica (gold standard, highest yield in weeks 1–2)
Widal Agglutination Serology Test (evaluating baseline TO & TH antibody titers)
Typhidot (IgM & IgG serology rapid antibody assay)
Stool & Urine Cultures for Salmonella isolation
Complete Liver Function Test (LFT) panel
doctor_discussion_points: Discuss travel history, food/water exposure, or recent dining outside.
Evaluate whether empirical antibiotic therapy (such as azithromycin, ceftriaxone, or fluoroquinolones) is indicated pending culture results.
Review hydration, oral rehydration therapy (ORS), and temperature management.

biomarker_rules.description: Marked or progressive thrombocytopenia (low platelet count)
Pronounced leukopenia (low white blood cell count)
Elevated transaminases from acute viral stress

overview: Dengue is an acute mosquito-borne viral infection marked by a sharp drop in platelets (thrombocytopenia), low white blood cells (leukopenia), and sometimes elevated hematocrit reflecting plasma leakage. Daily monitoring of platelet count and hematocrit is standard clinical protocol.
suggested_follow_up_tests: Dengue NS1 Antigen ELISA (high diagnostic sensitivity during days 1–5 of fever)
Dengue IgM & IgG Antibody ELISA (identifies primary vs. secondary infection after day 5)
Serial Complete Blood Counts (CBC) every 24 hours to monitor platelet trajectory and hematocrit stability
Serum Electrolytes and Liver Function Test
doctor_discussion_points: Watch for critical warning signs: persistent vomiting, severe abdominal tenderness, mucosal bleeding, or sudden restlessness.
Strict avoidance of NSAIDs, aspirin, or ibuprofen (acetaminophen/paracetamol is preferred to avoid worsening bleeding risks).
Aggressive oral hydration and electrolyte fluid management.

overview: The triad of low hemoglobin, low MCV, and low MCH indicates microcytic hypochromic red blood cells. The most prevalent cause globally is iron deficiency due to inadequate dietary intake, heavy menstrual blood loss, or occult gastrointestinal bleeding.
suggested_follow_up_tests: Serum Ferritin (most reliable indicator of total body iron stores)
Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) and Transferrin Saturation
Peripheral Blood Smear (PBS) microscopy to confirm microcytosis and anisopoikilocytosis
Fecal Occult Blood Test (FOBT) or endoscopy/colonoscopy if gastrointestinal blood loss is suspected
doctor_discussion_points: Determine the underlying cause of iron loss or malabsorption rather than treating numbers in isolation.
Discuss oral iron supplementation regimens (e.g. ferrous sulfate or bisglycinate with Vitamin C for optimal absorption).
Explore dietary enrichment with heme and non-heme iron sources.

condition_name: Vitamin B12 or Folate Deficiency (Macrocytic Anemia)

biomarker_rules.description: Macrocytosis (abnormally large red blood cells > 100 fL)

overview: Macrocytic anemia with elevated MCV often stems from impaired DNA synthesis during erythrocyte maturation, most frequently driven by Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency may also cause neurological and sensory symptoms.
suggested_follow_up_tests: Serum Vitamin B12 and Serum Folate quantification
Methylmalonic Acid (MMA) and Homocysteine levels (sensitive functional metabolic markers)
Intrinsic Factor Antibodies & Parietal Cell Antibodies (to evaluate Pernicious Anemia)
Peripheral Blood Smear for hypersegmented neutrophils
doctor_discussion_points: Assess dietary patterns (e.g., strict vegetarian/vegan diets) and gastric absorption issues (e.g., prolonged metformin or PPI use).
Discuss parenteral (IM) or high-dose oral cobalamin replacement.
Review any sensory or neurological symptoms (tingling, gait imbalance).

biomarker_rules.description: Leukocytosis (elevated total white blood cell count)

overview: A marked elevation in total WBC count accompanied by neutrophilia is the quintessential hallmark of acute bacterial infection, tissue injury, or systemic inflammation. Identification of the anatomical focus of infection is essential.
suggested_follow_up_tests: High-sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hs-CRP) and Quantitative Procalcitonin
Targeted Cultures: Urine Analysis & Culture, Sputum, Throat Swab, or Wound Swab
Chest Radiograph (X-ray) if pulmonary signs (cough, dyspnea) are present
Blood cultures if high-grade spikes or bacteremia is suspected
doctor_discussion_points: Identify the specific anatomical site of infection (respiratory, urinary, skin, dental, etc.).
Determine whether targeted antimicrobial therapy is warranted based on culture sensitivity.
Monitor temperature curves and vital signs.

biomarker_rules.description: Hyperglycemia (fasting glucose exceeding normal physiological baseline)

overview: Elevated fasting blood sugar and/or HbA1c indicates impaired insulin secretion or systemic insulin resistance. Prediabetes (HbA1c 5.7–6.4%) and Diabetes (HbA1c ≥ 6.5% or FPG ≥ 126 mg/dL) require structured lifestyle, nutritional, and medical management.
suggested_follow_up_tests: Confirmatory Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) and 2-Hour Postprandial Glucose (PPBS)
Standardized 75g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT)
Urine Spot Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio (uACR) for renal microvascular screening
Comprehensive Lipid Panel and baseline ECG
doctor_discussion_points: Personalized glycemic targets and home blood glucose self-monitoring.
Medical nutrition therapy (low glycemic index carbohydrates, fiber enrichment).
Evaluation for first-line pharmacotherapy (e.g. metformin) or lifestyle modification programs.

biomarker_rules.description: Secondary hypercholesterolemia due to lowered metabolic clearance

overview: An elevated TSH level is the most sensitive indicator that the thyroid gland is producing inadequate thyroxine. If Free T4 is normal, this is subclinical hypothyroidism; if Free T4 is reduced, it indicates overt hypothyroidism, commonly caused by autoimmune Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
suggested_follow_up_tests: Free T4 and Free T3 quantitative blood levels
Anti-Thyroid Peroxidase (Anti-TPO) & Anti-Thyroglobulin (Anti-Tg) Antibodies
High-resolution Thyroid Ultrasound imaging
Lipid panel evaluation
doctor_discussion_points: Whether thyroid hormone replacement therapy (levothyroxine) is recommended based on TSH threshold.
Timing of medication (taken fasting in the morning away from calcium or iron supplements).
Schedule for repeat TSH testing in 6–8 weeks for dosage titration.

overview: Suppressed TSH alongside elevated Free T4 reflects an overactive thyroid gland (thyrotoxicosis), most commonly driven by Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goiter, or subacute thyroiditis.
suggested_follow_up_tests: Free T3 (Triiodothyronine) quantitative assessment
TSH Receptor Antibodies (TRAb) / Thyroid Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSI)
Radioactive Iodine Uptake (RAIU) and thyroid scan
Baseline Electrocardiogram (ECG) for rhythm evaluation
doctor_discussion_points: Symptom management with beta-blockers for tachycardia and tremors.
Evaluation of antithyroid medications (e.g. methimazole or propylthiouracil).
Endocrinology consultation for specialized management.

overview: A pattern of elevated LDL, high triglycerides, and low HDL is associated with increased deposition of arterial plaques (atherosclerosis) and elevated long-term cardiovascular risk.
suggested_follow_up_tests: Apolipoprotein B (ApoB) and Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)]
High-sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hs-CRP) for vascular inflammation
Coronary Artery Calcium (CAC) CT scan for structural plaque assessment
10-Year ASCVD (Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease) Risk Score calculation
doctor_discussion_points: Calculation of comprehensive 10-year ASCVD risk score.
Need for lipid-lowering pharmacotherapy (e.g. statin therapy, ezetimibe).
Cardiovascular risk reduction through diet, physical exercise, and blood pressure monitoring.

biomarker_rules.description: Elevated ALT reflecting liver cell membrane disruption
Elevated AST from hepatic or metabolic stress

overview: Transaminase elevations (ALT and AST) indicate hepatocellular stress or injury. Common benign and reversible causes include metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (fatty liver / MASLD), acute medication/supplement effects, alcohol, or viral hepatitis.
suggested_follow_up_tests: Abdominal Ultrasound (assessing liver echogenicity, hepatomegaly, and fatty infiltration)
Viral Hepatitis Serology Panel (HBsAg for Hepatitis B, Anti-HCV for Hepatitis C, HAV IgM)
Fractionated Bilirubin and Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT)
Serum Ferritin and iron saturation to rule out hemochromatosis
doctor_discussion_points: Review of all prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, herbal remedies, and alcohol intake.
Lifestyle and dietary interventions focused on gradual weight reduction and metabolic control.
Timing for repeat liver panel in 4–8 weeks.

condition_name: Renal Impairment / Early Chronic Kidney Stress

biomarker_rules.description: Elevated serum creatinine reflecting reduced filtration
Hyperkalemia due to decreased tubular excretion

overview: Elevated creatinine and BUN indicate reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Causes range from reversible prerenal dehydration and medication nephrotoxicity to primary renal parenchymal conditions.
suggested_follow_up_tests: Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) and Serum Cystatin C
Urine Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio (uACR) and Complete Urinalysis with Microscopy
Renal & Bladder Ultrasound (measuring kidney size, cortical thickness, and obstruction)
Serum Electrolytes (Sodium, Potassium, Bicarbonate, Calcium, Phosphate)
doctor_discussion_points: Distinguish between acute kidney injury (e.g., dehydration, NSAID use) and chronic changes.
Review blood pressure targets and nephroprotective medications (such as ACEi/ARB or SGLT2i).
Avoidance of nephrotoxic medications (including regular NSAIDs/ibuprofen, contrast dyes).

overview: A low platelet count reduces normal hemostatic clot formation. Common causes include acute viral infections (such as Dengue or viral hepatitis), immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), drug-induced suppression, or splenic sequestration.
suggested_follow_up_tests: Repeat CBC with Manual Peripheral Blood Smear to rule out EDTA-dependent pseudothrombocytopenia (platelet clumping)
Coagulation Profile (PT/INR and aPTT)
Viral serologies (Dengue, Hepatitis B/C, HIV, EBV)
Immune workup (Antinuclear Antibodies, Direct Coombs Test if indicated)
doctor_discussion_points: Review of recent medications (e.g. heparin, quinine, anticonvulsants, certain antibiotics).
Bleeding precaution counseling (avoid contact sports, avoid aspirin/NSAIDs).
Urgent hematology referral if platelet count is significantly decreased (< 50,000 /mcL).
